title: WannaCry: 59 days, a worm, and an unexpected brake.
description: A Friday outbreak, a fix released 59 days earlier, and a researcher’s domain registration that changed the story.

sources.title: Microsoft · WannaCry technical analysis
sources.note: Worm propagation through vulnerable SMB services; behavior of the domain check.

sources.title: Microsoft · MS17-010 bulletin, 14 March 2017
sources.note: The security update preceded the 12 May outbreak by 59 days.

sources.title: Marcus Hutchins · the domain discovery
sources.note: First-hand account; the domain check affected particular samples, not every possible variant.

sources.title: UK Parliament · impact on the NHS
sources.note: Cancelled appointments and diverted patients in England.

html:
INCIDENT FILE / 001WANNACRY · 2017
01 / THE OUTBREAK

Friday. Files locked.
Hospitals disrupted.

12 May 2017. Windows PCs around the world display ransom demands. In England, hospitals cancel appointments and divert patients.

The malware has a name: WannaCry.

02 / THE CHAIN REACTION

One infected PC.
Then the next.

WannaCry paired file-encrypting ransomware with a worm: code that could spread between vulnerable computers.

Using the EternalBlue exploit against unpatched Windows SMB services, an infected machine could seek out more victims. Each new infection could keep the chain going, without another person clicking an attachment.

03 / THE HEAD START

The fix was already
59 days old.

Microsoft released the MS17-010 security update on 14 March. The outbreak began on 12 May.

For affected systems still missing that fix, those 59 days had not become protection.

The March update covered supported Windows versions; emergency legacy updates followed in May.

04 / THE UNEXPECTED BRAKE

Then a researcher
registered a domain.

Analyzing WannaCry, researcher Marcus Hutchins noticed a request to an unregistered domain. He registered it to help track the malware.

The twist: when the checked domain responded successfully, the affected sample stopped before running its ransomware and spreading further.

05 / THE TAKEAWAY

A brake on the spread.
No undo button.

Making that domain reachable interrupted affected samples. It did not decrypt files already locked, and variants could change or remove the check.

WannaCry leaves two memorable details: a fix waiting to be deployed, and a small discovery that bought defenders time.

Why the patch gap matters

Publishing an update does not install it across an organization. WannaCry made that gap painfully visible. The lesson: the security work continues after a fix ships. It has to reach the systems that need it.

1 / 5

A historical explainer. Primary sources are in the Archive’s Sources menu.
